source_span: the composite PMI unexpectedly hit a 5-year high of 58.4 in September (vs. 55.3 expected)... which in turn would enable the Fed to keep hiking rates to deal with inflation
source_chain: Strong September composite PMI (58.4 vs 55.3 expected) plus an oil rebound therefore hawkish Fed repricing (71% odds of an October hike, 37bp of 2026 hikes priced) therefore the biggest one-day Treasury yield jump since April 2025, 10Y to a post-2007 high of 5.11%, reinforced by a weak 5Y auction tail (JPM's afternoon briefing, 17537: 3.20bp tail, weakest input-cost rise since 2020) therefore equities sell off despite the good growth print because a higher-for-longer rate path punctures valuations. No single stated break condition; DB frames this as the recurring pattern of markets under-pricing hikes until data forces a correction.
pulse_chain: Reproduces the same activity-to-policy-to-yield-to-equity chain with correct per-bank sourcing: PMI beat, 10Y level and Fed pricing to Deutsche Bank; the 3.20bp auction tail and the input-cost jump to JPMorgan, matching 17537 verbatim. It layers in JPMorgan's countervailing thesis from the separate international briefing (17539: 5.5% fair value, 'similar episodes have historically been buying opportunities,' tactically cautious view) correctly attributed to JPM, then closes on an editorial invalidation (Sept 30 PCE as the real-vs-artifact test, 5.5% as the level that settles the debate) that neither source states outright but that contradicts nothing either bank argues.
why: Every directional claim and figure is attributed to the bank that actually made it (DB for the PMI/yield/pricing chain, JPM for the auction tail and the 5.5% fair-value counter-thesis) with no step reversed or reassigned, so the chain holds even though the closing Sept-30/5.5% invalidation is the pulse's own synthesis rather than a line either note wrote.
